Special to the Nashville American.

MURFREESBORO, July 18.—Houston Turner, colored, who outraged Miss O'Neal, was captured at 1 p.m. today, near Smyrna, in this county, by Moore Batty, colored. Two other negroes were in close pursuit, whom Turner was keeping at a distance by threatening them with a long stick, the only weapon he has carried since committing the deed. Batty met him and presented a musket in his face, and he surrendered promptly. He was identified by parties in the neighborhood, and brought here on the 5.30 tram, this evening, and lodged in jail. Turner is a slender-build, copper-colored negro, and says he is nineteen years old. He committed the deed on the 8th inst., since which time different parties have been in pursuit of him every day, and he has been seen by some one who knew him almost every day. He has not been exceeding fifteen miles from Murfreesboro during the time, and whenever seen, did not seem to be making any special effort to conceal himself, but always managed to evade his pursuers. On the 14th he was arrested by parties near Eagleville, but escaped. On Saturday last he was chased and fired at several times, but escaped. He says he was in Murfreesboro Saturday evening and bought some tobacco on the public square. This, I think, is doubtful. When arrested he gave his name as Wm. Davis, and said he had never been in the neighborhood where the crime was committed. Since being brought there he has been identified by fully one hundred people, to all of whom he gave the same reply, that he knew nothing of the crime, but in an interview with him to-night, when told that probably he would be in eternity before daylight to-morrow, he

ACKNOWLEDGED THE CRIME,

stating that he saw Miss O'Neal as she went to the neighbor's house and waited on the roadside until she returned, when he pulled her off her horse and took her into the woods and committed the deed. He said, when she attempted to scream for help, he caught her by the throat to prevent. Since his lodgment in jail the crowd has been increasing around the jail, and the street leading from the jail to the public square by nine o'clock was thronged, at which time, it being evident, that if he remained in jail he would be mobbed before morning, the jail door was opened and Sheriffs Ransoms and Majors, with pistols in hand,

RUSHED THE PRISONER
out and hustled him into a buggy and started at full speed out the Nashville pike, intending to run him off to Nashville for safe keeping. When they had gotten near the river, about a mile from town, a mob of about one hundred men closed in on all sides and demanded the prisoner, and, before any resistance could be made, the sheriff and prisoner were in the hands of tha mob, and by main staeength were prevented from making further efforts to protect the prisoner. In a few minutes the mob returned quietly to

THE PUBLIC SQUARE,
on foot, and proceeded immediately to the court-house yard, placed out sentinels on all sides, who kept back the large crowd collected, and without a word being uttered above an ordinary voice, hanged the rav isher to a small sycamore. After a few moments the mob fell into line, and in the same quiet manner marched out West Main street. At this hour, 10.30, Houston Turne, colored, the ravisher of Miss Mary O'Neal, still hangs, and probably will not be cut down before morning.

The last Legislature passed a law to
take the sense of the people of the State as to the necessity of calling a Convention to revise the Constitution, and accordingly the question will be voted on at the August election. Article XII of the Constitution as it stands provides that, when a majority of the members of the two Houses of the Legislature within the first twenty days of the session, concur, they may pass a law to take the sense of the people as to the necessity of calling a Convention. The question shall be submitted to the people at the next general election, and if a majority of all the voters of the State vote therefor, at the next meeting of the Legislature the question shall a second time be submitted to the people, and if a majority of the voters favor the proposition, the Legislature must call a Constitutional Convention.

This section renders it almost an impossibility to ever change the document, and its makers were thus particular with reference to a change so that no interference could be made in regard to slavery, much feared at the time. That institution having been abolished, all laws in reference to it have become dead letters, while a change in the times has rendered many other of the articles void and inoperative. That there is a necessity for a revision no thinking man will deny, and, this being the case, it becomes the people to turn out en masse and vote to call a Convention. The question has been put to the people several times, but owing to the failure of the masses to understand or to care whether a change is made or not, the necessary majority of all the voters in the State has never been obtained. We fear a like result will follow the coming effort to get a majority. The people have it in their power to vote on either side of the question, and if they fail to vote at all it is hardly fair that it should be taken that they are opposed to the change. Every effort should be made to poll as large a vote as possible, but if it is largely in favor of calling the Convention and does not reach the necessary majority, it should become the duty of the next Legislature to take revolutionary measures toward a change, by appointing the time and place for holding a Convention and asking the people to send delegates to it. The duty of such a Convention would be to make the needed changes in the Constitution, and it would then remain for the people to adopt or reject it at the polls. We wish that every voter could be made to understand the importance of his vote in the matter, and we suggest that officers of the election take special pains to ask each man to vote on the question.

An Epidemic of Crime.

It really does seem that the country is experiencing the evil effects of a moral collapse of unexampled character. Not a week, a day—nay, an hour—passes by without some revelation of a desperate crime being made. No section of the country is free from lawless deeds; no class of society is exempt from the presence of the crimson stains of violence. Thoughtful people are roused by the number and startling character of the crimes which are being committed everywhere. The germs of the epidemic seem to pervade the whole moral atmosphere; corrupting, enraging and nerving the victims of the disorder to deeds of death. The crime craze has reached the higher social circles, and all sorts of scandals and peccadillos result therefrom. Indeed, among the high and the low, the rich and the poor, the learned and the unlearned, there seems to have been a complete letting down of moral principle; and instead of peace and safety, a reign of crime has been inaugurated. The records of a single day's development of crime would fill a volume. To day, a negro in Louisiana attempts a dastardly outrage on a young lady; to morrow morning's sun will greet a ghastly corpse swinging to the limb of a tree. A jail guard in Arkansas opens the door of the prison and allows a quartette of dangerous desperadoes to go their way. In another part of the same State, a howling mob takes from the jail a prisoner under a long sentence, shoot, and then hang him. In Rutherford county, Tennessee, a negro man, for a brutal outrage, is seized by a mob of lynchers, and speedily dispatched. Two murders and one legal execution took place in Arkansas last Friday, and on the same day two men were killed in affrays, one hanged by the officers of the law in Henry county, Missouri, while at Maryville, in the same State, two youths, convicted of the crime of killing their own father, were put to death by the Sheriff in accordance with the sentence of a court. In Texas several persons were wounded and bruised in affrays, and some were killed outright on this same fatal Friday. We read of Italian bandits domiciled in New Orleans, and the next instant our eyes behold the bloody records of American brigands, who stopped a whole train, killed the conductor and a passenger, and carried away the contents of the express safe. But we have no disposition to extend the list further. It is a sickening record. The crimes include every variety and grade. Crime against life, against property, against virtue, against morality; the violent struggle of infuriated men, the stealthy shot of the concealed assassins; the pitiless embrace of the lusty brute; the invasion of the sanctities of home; slanders and lapses of every grade and character constitute a part of the records of the crimes of a week.

What can be the matter? Is the moral world out of joint? May there not be some subtle influence—some atmospheric conditions that act upon the cerebral organs to produce a species of madness? Whether that be the case or not, certain it is that the country seems to be afflicted with an epidemic of crime, such as his never before swept over it. The moral tone of the people and the press appear to be low. Mob law is justified and defended by public prints, and deeds of violence seem to excite but a passing consideration. Something must be done to check the reign of lawlessness. What is the cause? No remedy can be applied without a knowledge of the nature of the disease.

The Railroad War.
NEW YORK, July 26th.—The warfare in passenger rates is likely to continue for some time to come. All the roads are selling this morning at $8 to Chicago, $7 50 to Cincinnati and $13 70 to St. Louis. At half-past 10 General Samuel Carpenter, ticket agent of the Pennsylvania Central Railroad, ordered all the ticket offices on his line to sell tickets to Chicago for $8, Cincinnati 7 50, St. Louis $13 25. He said that they would not be undersold by scalpers or by other lines, and they could keep up the fight as long as anybody.

New Telegraph Company.
CHICAGO, July 26th.—A New York special says: A new telegraph company has been formed by well known capitalists in this country and in Europe. It is intended that it shall include every paying point covered by the Western Union lines. It is understood that James R. Keene is to be President. The Directors will include John Mackey, of the Comstock lode, and other well known California capitalists. George D. Roberts is also largely interested in the new company. The capital will be about $10,000,000 in money, and it is asserted that it is already subscribed. The lines are to be constructed on a pure cash basis, and be furnished with all modern improvements. A meeting is to be held to-morrow by those interested.

The Chinese Students.
CHEYENE (Wyo.), July 26th.—The Leader to-morrow will contain an interview with Teu Soon Kee, an attache of the Chinese Embassy at Washington. He says that the Chinese students withdrawn from America will be sent to England, France and Germany. They number 100. The Chinese Government will hereafter educate its students in Europe and China, where military and naval schools are being established. The inference drawn by the interviewer is that the Chinese Government fears the progressiveness of American institutions. Teu Soon Kee says the new Embassy, headed by Jum Tsou Roo, will go to Washington in December.

JUDGE LYNCH.
A Fiend Attempts to Carry out a Hellish Design, is Foiled and Afterwards Pays the Penalty With his Life.
On last Wednesday night two weeks ago, one of the most diabolical plans was sought to be carried out that has ever been attempted in Lincoln parish in many a day. Mr. A. J. Taylor resides in the Southern part of this parish, about seven miles from Vienna. He has had living with him this year a negro man by the name of Silas Lee who was an ordinary farm hand on the place. Several weeks ago Mr. Taylor went to Texas in order to improve his health, leaving with his family two young men to look after his business and protect his family. On the night above mentioned, some time about the middle or latter part, Mrs. Taylor was aroused from her slumbers by a noise in her room, which she occupied with two or three of her children, among whom was her oldest daughter a girl twelve or fifteen years of age, she arose and lit her lamp for the purpose of ascertaining the cause of the noise which appeared to be at the bed of her daughter and upon approaching the bed she saw and recognized this negro man Silas Lee lying under her daughters bed in a perfectly nude state. Mrs. Taylor screamed several times but, seems without arousing the young men woo were occupying a room remote from hers. Realizing that he was discovered and becoming alarmed the negro crawled from under the bed and ran off. It appears that Mrs. Taylor did not acquaint the young men and the balance of the family with the fact until next morning. No effort was made to arrest him by the young men on the place the next day, for fear he would get away, although he appeared on the place several times during the day and showing by his actions and looks that he was in constant fear of something. On that night (Thursday night) there was a negro wedding in the neighborhood. Silas Lee not being on hand was sent for by some one in the woods near by to come out and help doctor a sick horse; he went and was there met by a crowd and marched off to an old field, tied and literally filled with buckshot and left as dead, supposedly, as he would ever be. But he was not dead yet. After the crowd left him he managed to untie himself and crawl to a negro shanty, not far off, and there remained until Saturday evening, when Dr. Null was sent for. By this time his case was hopeless on account of the severity of his wounds and the time that had elapsed since he was shot that he was without medical aid, one of his arms being literally shattered and his body filled with shot. Saturday night he was again taken out and this time he was dispatched in short order.

He was found the next day about five hundred yards from Mr. A. H. Riter's, in a piece of woods, at which place Coroner C. H. Griffin held an inquest over his body. Thus did he pay the penalty his act so richly deserved. While we do not approve of lynch law as generally applicable to all flagrant violations of criminal law, yet we do approve of it when applied to cases like the present. The chances of escape are two great to allow such a fiend the benefit of a trial by jury and the sooner such characters are taught the necessary consequences of such acts the better it will be for them and the community at large. This villain has been guilty of several attempts before, he was shot in Ouachita parish several years ago and ned from Jackson to Lincoln for fear of punishment for a similar offense to his last attempted, while in Jackson. His end came none too early nor too tragic, considering the heinousness of the crime he was attempting to perpetrate.

RIOTOUS NEGROES.
Firing Into a Pleasure Party of Ladies and Gentlemen in Louisiana—Sixteen Men Arrested and two Held for Murder.

NEW ORLEANS, August 23, 1881.

On Saturday last a party of young ladies and gentleman gathered at the residence of Mrs. J. B. Garone, at False River parish of Pointe Coupe, to pass the evening. It appears that the negroes of the upper part of the parish had chosen the same night to have a ball in a building which is just opposite Mrs. Garone's, on the premises of Mr. David Johnson and close to the residence. The negroes were very boisterous, and when the party at Garone's broke up, Johnson, Mr. Chenvert and two or three others walked over to the building, and Johnson told the negroes if they could not behave themselves they must leave. Then the negroes seemed to settle down, and the group of gentlemen stood on the opposite side of the road and watched developments. The negroes gathered in front of the schoolhouse, where their ball had been in progress, speaking in subdued whispers.

Suddenly a negro exploded his pistol in the air, and at once the negroes opened a terrific and indiscriminate fire on the whites. Mr. Cenvert snatched Johnson's pistol from him and returned the fire, and as he did so he fell shot through the heart. Johnson ran to get his gun, the negroes directed their fire against him. Fortunately he escaped without injury. While Johnson was running for his gun Mr. Joseph Garon hearing the firing got his pistol and went to the rescue. As soon as he appeared the fire of the negroes was turned upon him, and he fell wounded in the thigh, but rose and returned the fire. Then he attempted to climb the fence so as to get under cover. Ere he reached the railing, however, he received another ball under the shoulderblade and fell to the ground. Mr. Johnson now came up and fired upon the negroes, when they scattered and fled in every direction. Several of them were wounded, and sixteen were afterward arrested. All of these were discharged, with the exception of Val Nowal and Leopold Polite, who are ordered to be held on a charge of murder.

Negro Riot and Bloodshed in Pointe Coupee Parish.
The Pointe Coupee Banner says there was a negro riot on False River in that parish on the night of the 13th inst. A party of young ladies and gentlemen had assembled at the residence of Mrs. J. B. Garon, and in a building about one hundred feet distant a negro ball was being given. About midnight, as the party at Mrs. Garon's was about to break up, a row occurred among the negroes at the neighboring ball, and their curses became so fierce and noisy that Mr. L. T. Chenvert and three or four other gentlemen, including Mr. David Johnson, who had permitted the negroes to give the ball, went to the building where the ball was being given, and Mr. Johnson informed the negroes that if they could not preserve order they would have to leave the premises. The latter, after a brief consultation among themselves, made a rush on the white men, and commenced firing at them with pistols. The whites were unarmed, except Mr. Johnson. Mr. Chenvert snatched Mr. Johnson's pistol and fired one shot at the negroes, and at the same time one of the negroes shot Mr. Chenvert through the head, killing him instantly. Mr. Johnson ran to his house for his gun, among a shower of bullets from the negroes, and at the same time Joseph Garon, aged 18 years, ran up to the crowd with a pistol, and was shot down by the negroes. On Saturday evening, the 13th inst., a party of young ladies and gentlemen had gathered at the residence of Mrs. J. B. Garon, on False River, where they were to have a night gumbo and where they spent the evening in pleasant amusement; and it seems that the negroes of upper False River had chosen the same night to have a ball in the building formerly used as a negro school-house which is about one hundred feet from the residence of Mrs. Garon and situated on premises at present occupied by Mr. David Johnson (white,) Mr. Johnson's residence being about forty feet from the school-house and on the opposite side from Mrs. Garons. Mr. Chenvert and two other gentlemen who were at Mrs. Garon's walked over to Mr. Johnson's during the night, between eleven and twelve o'clock, when the party at Mrs. Garon's was about to break up some of the negroes at the ball began a fuss and loud cursing whereupon Mr. Johnson, Mr. Chenvert and the other two or three who were with them walked over, and Mr. Johnson said to the negroes that he had only consented for them to have their ball there on condition that everything was to be conducted in an orderly and quiet manner, and that if they could not behave themselves they would have to quit the premises. After this there was apparent quiet for a moment, the few whites remaining standing on the opposite side of the road from the school-house, and a crowd of negroes just in front of the building on the narrow plot of ground between it and the road, the negroes being in consultation among themselves in a subdued tone, when suddenly one of the negroes fired his pistol in the air, and a voice was heard crying 'come quick boys let's crowd them and give them hell,' when the crowd of negroes opened a terrific and indiscriminate fire on the whites. Mr. Johnson being the only one among the latter who had an arm, a pistol, which Mr. Chenvert grabbed from him and returned the fire of the negroes by one shot, which he had no sooner done than he fell dead, he being shot through the heart by a large sized bullet. As Chenvert fell, one of the gentlemen present cried out 'for God sake, Johnson, get your gun, and Mr. Johnson ran for his house, as he did so the whole fire of the negroes was turned upon him, but fortunately he escaped without injury, although the fence near his gate was badly splintered by the flying and murderous balls.

About the time Mr. Johnson ran for his gun, young Joseph Garon, a youth, about 18 years of age, who was at his mother's, hearing what was going on, picked up his pistol and ran out to the rescue; but as soon as he came in sight the fire of the negroes was turned upon him and he fell from a ball through the thigh, he rose, however, and returned the fire of the negroes, and then seeing the disadvantage under which he was placed, tried to get over the fence on the roadside so as to fight under cover, but as he got on to the fence he received another ball under the shoulder blade which completely disabled him, he falling on the field side, and as soon as he did so Johnson came out with his double-barrel gun, which was loaded with No. 7 shot, and fired first one barrel and then the other into the crowd of negroes, when they scattered and dispersed in every direction.

Several of the negroes were slightly wounded by bird shot, and one was wounded by a ball in the flesh covering of the abdomen. As the news spread on Sunday a large crowd gathered in New Road by Sunday afternoon, every one being anxious to take the necessary steps to catch and punish the assassins; but it was with great difficulty that information could be obtained as to who were the negroes that participated in the affair, it being evident that there were at least fifteen or twenty of them, as they had fired between fifty and a hundred shots. As soon as sufficient information was obtained, squads started in every direction in search of the guilty, and up to the present writing sixteen negroes have been brought to jail as implicated in the affair, and there are some four or five of the most guilty still at large, several of them supposed to have escaped from the parish. Of those arrested some were found hiding in the woods, in field ditches and other out-of-the-way places. At this hour of writing, 1 o'clock P. M., Friday, a preliminary examination of those arrested is being held before Judge Yoist at the court house, and what will be the result we cannot predict; but it is certain that there is a fixed determination on the part of the white population that the guilty shall not escape full measure of punishment. The stores are all closed and business suspended.

On the 29th of June, in the joy of their honeymoon, Dr. Mitchell was walking up the road near his country home, when he beheld what almost paralyzed him with horror. His lovely wife lay before him a ghastly corpse. Her throat was cut from ear to ear, and her body wrs torn with the fearful clutches of her murderer. It was discovered that she had been raped and murdered. The neighborhood was at once aflame with excitement, and search for the guilty wretch was begun. Jesse Waldrop had not long been in the county, but there had followed him rumors of his bad character. He was seen on the road near where the corpse was found on the day of the murder. With these evidences search for him was begun at once, and it was found that he had fled. Late yesterday afternoon the scene of the murder was reached. Nothing was done rashly, but preparations were made for the execution with ghastly coolness. Waldrop was firmly tied and bound with wire to a stake driven on the spot where his victim was found, when for the first time his dogged courage failed. He pleaded piteously, not for life, but only to be allowed to die by the gallows or bullet; but he cried to men of stone and at midnight one of the relatives of the unfortunate woman applied the torch to the pine which saturated with oil had been piled around him. His screams rang out on the quiet country air, and the flames lit up the scene with lurid glare. The death struggles were horrid, but not a man stirred. Standing in a circle around the human sacrifice, they looked with stolid indifference on the horrid expiation of the crime. From first to last the officers made no effort to save the prisoner for a legal doom. If they had it would have been futile, for popular passion was fairly frenzied. Waldrop was twenty-three years old, and a man of good address.

waldrop-1881-07.A27:
Swift and Terrible Retribution. On the 90th of June in Rendelph
On the 29th of June, in Randolph county Georgia, Mrs. Carrie Mitchell, a beautiful and accomplished young married lady, was found by her husband in the road near their home with her throat cut from ear to ear and her person otherwise brutally abused. Suspicion pointed strongly to one Jas. Waldrop, a notorious and desperate character who was seen in the neighborhood that morning, and a party of determined men immediately started on the track of the scoundrel and followed him up so successfully that they captured him near Newman Ala., on the night of the 3d, inst. The guilty wretch fought desperately but was finally secured, finding all hope of escape gone he made a full confession, giving all the horrible details of his assault on the poor innocent victim, her resistance, his brutal passion, the murder and his accomplishing his hellish purpose when his victim was in the throes of death. The indignant and horror-struck hearers took him back to the scene of his crime and binding him to a stake with wire, piled pine knots, saturated with oil, around him and burned him to death and his body to ashes. Who shall say his punishment was not just?
waldrop-1881-07.A35:
Accusation by a Dying Murderer.
ATLANTA, (Ga.), July 19.—It has transpired that, as Jesse Waldrop was lynched for the murder of Mrs. Al. Mitchell, he called to him Hal Mitchell, in the same county, who was not living with his wife at the time, and said: "Hal, you know you promised to give me $75, and you have caused me to lose my sweet life. I am going to die in a few minutes. I don't fear death as much as you ought to fear the falsehoods you have told to cause my death. I was to kill Mrs. Hal Mitchell, and I mistook the name for Mrs. Al. Mitchell. You promised me $75 if I would commit the horrid deed, and you promised you would give me $25 more if I killed an old man as you intended. I killed Mrs. Mitchell by mistake, supposing she was the woman who swore against me, and whom you wanted me to kill. I have mistaken my victim, but I go to my God with this confession on my lips."
